claims.text: Conventional high-entropy alloys are composed largely of heavier elements.
Conventional high-entropy alloys combine high strength with relatively high density.
Partially substituting heavier alloying elements with a higher fraction of aluminum increases the lightweight-element fraction.
Increasing the aluminum fraction will reduce the alloy's overall density.
Increasing the aluminum fraction will produce or preserve a single-phase material.
The modified alloy will retain or improve both mechanical strength and ductility.
The proposed performance will hold under ambient to moderately elevated temperatures and aerospace or automotive mechanical loading.
The modified alloy will possess a homogeneous, stabilized single-phase microstructure.
High configurational entropy maintains the homogeneous single-phase microstructure.
The multicomponent high-entropy alloy exhibits intrinsic lattice distortion because its constituent elements have different atomic sizes.
Intrinsic lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion.
The combination of reduced density and controlled defect mobility allows strength and ductility to be maintained or improved.
The modified alloy will show a measurable density decrease relative to the baseline alloy.
The modified alloy will maintain or improve strength and ductility relative to the baseline alloy.
Composition and annealing temperature can control whether an aluminum-containing high-entropy alloy remains single phase or decomposes into B2 and BCC phases.
Increasing aluminum beyond an optimal level may trigger phase separation or other microstructural instability.
Phase decomposition can alter mechanical properties.
The aluminum fraction and processing parameters required to preserve a unified phase are not yet specified.

contradictions.description: The experiment proposes systematically increasing aluminum content while maintaining constant overall elemental proportions. Overall proportions cannot remain constant if aluminum's proportion changes; the design should instead specify which elements are reduced or state that only the ratios among the non-aluminum elements remain constant.
